e.meaning: from Horatius, a Roman family name of uncertain meaning
e.etymology: From Latin Horatius, a Roman family name of obscure, possibly Etruscan, origin. It honors the poet Quintus Horatius Flaccus, known in English as Horace.
namesakes: Horace Grant (NBA champion with the Bulls)

e.etymology: A German pet form of Maria that became an English name in the 20th century, helped by stage names such as Mitzi Green and Mitzi Gaynor.
namesakes: Mitzi Gaynor (actress and dancer, South Pacific)

e.etymology: A less common spelling of Melanie, from French Mélanie and Latin Melania, the name of two fifth-century saints, from Greek melas, black or dark.

e.meaning: short form of names ending in -lita
e.etymology: A short form of names that end in -lita, such as Carmelita, Estrellita and Lolita, where -ita is the Spanish ending for little.
A spelling of Jacqueline, the French feminine of Jacques, which comes from Jacob and James. Jacob is traditionally read as holder of the heel or supplanter.
An English occupational surname for a gardener, from Old Northern French gardinier, used as a first name since the 1800s.
A spelling of Tiana, which began as a short form of Tatiana and Christiana. Tyana was also an ancient city in Cappadocia.
A short form of Dorotea, the Dorothea of Italian and the Nordic and Slavic languages, from Greek for gift of God; a sister of Thea. Actress Téa Leoni made it familiar in the US in the 1990s.
e.note: Without an accent it reads as the drink tea, so expect it to be said as one syllable.

assoc.t: tea, the drink, spelled the same

e.etymology: A spelling of Aimee, from French Aimée, beloved, the source of English Amy. Aimé is the French masculine form, and Aime is also an Estonian girls' name.
A short form of Matilda, from Germanic maht, might, and hild, battle.
An English and Scottish surname, probably from a pet form of Patrick. The 1985 western Silverado, with Kevin Kline as the gunman Paden, put it into use as a first name.
An African-American coinage of the 1990s that joins the Ty- of Tyrone to the sound of Tariq; also spelled Tyreek and Tyreke.
Latin dea, goddess. It is a given name in Italy, Albania and Indonesia, and has also served as a short form of Dorothea.
e.note: In capitals it reads as DEA, the US Drug Enforcement Administration.

assoc.t: DEA, the US Drug Enforcement Administration

e.etymology: A respelling of Sammy, the pet form of Samantha and Samuel. Samuel is Hebrew, read as name of God or God has heard; Samantha is an 18th-century American feminine form.

e.meaning: from Laurentum, a city whose name is linked to laurel
e.etymology: A respelling of Lauren, the feminine form of Laurence, from Latin Laurentius, a man from Laurentum; the name has long been tied to laurus, the laurel of victors.

e.meaning: pet form of Maria; also the Latin word for mine
e.etymology: Used in the US as a spelling of Mia, a Scandinavian and German short form of Maria. Mea is also the Latin word for my or mine, as in mea culpa.

assoc.t: mea, Spanish for (he or she) urinates

e.etymology: A spelling of Chantal, from the title of Saint Jeanne de Chantal; the place name comes from Old Occitan cantal, stone. It is often linked to French chant, song, without basis.
An African-American coinage of the 1990s that joins the Da- prefix to Monte or stretches Damon. Damonte also exists as an Italian surname meaning from the mountain.

e.meaning: uncertain; traditionally read as exalted or high mountain
e.etymology: In the US a spelling of Aaron, the name of Moses's brother, whose origin is uncertain and may be Egyptian. Eron is separately an Icelandic name.
A respelling of Kennedy, from the Irish surname Ó Cinnéide, descendant of Cennétig, a byname made of ceann, head, and éidigh, helmeted or misshapen.

assoc.t: the Kennedy political family, same sound

e.etymology: A spelling of Aisha, from Arabic aisha, alive or living well. Aisha bint Abi Bakr was a wife of the Prophet Muhammad and a major source of hadith.
A longer spelling of Nakia, an American name of the 1970s; some families link it to Arabic naqiyya, pure.
From Triana, the riverside quarter of Seville known for flamenco and for its Virgin, Esperanza de Triana. Its use as a girl's name is modern.
A modern name with no single documented source; it reads as Kelly or Kaylee with the -ia ending of Celia and Delia.
A respelling of London, the English capital used as a first name. The city's name goes back to Roman Londinium; its earlier origin is unknown.

assoc.t: London, the capital of England, same sound

e.meaning: sound, cry; popularly glossed as peaceful
e.etymology: A spelling of Aarav, from Sanskrit arava, a sound or cry. Baby-name lists usually give it as peaceful, and it became one of the most popular boys' names in India in the 2000s.
A modern blend of the Jer- of Jeremy and Jerry with the ending of Eric or Derrick; also spelled Jerrick.
A modern spelling in the family of Leia, Laya and Leah, with the -iyah ending made popular by Aaliyah.
The Spanish and Italian form of Latin Aurelianus, from the Roman family name Aurelius, built on aureus, golden.
namesakes: Colonel Aureliano Buendía (hero of One Hundred Years of Solitude)

e.etymology: A spelling of Rainy or Rainey: the weather word, a pet form of Lorraine and Raine, or the Irish and Scottish surname Rainey.
A modern elaboration of Mia with the -ana ending, in the pattern of Liana and Kiana.

e.meaning: griffin, the mythical beast with an eagle's head and a lion's body
e.etymology: A spelling of Griffin taken from the legendary creature, whose name comes from Greek gryps. Griffin as a personal name also continues Welsh Gruffudd, Latinized as Griffinus.
